newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Suharto calls for unity after riot.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Suharto calls for unity after riot.

text.p: Indonesia's President Suharto appealed on Friday for unity and tolerance following riots in a West Java town where a mob of mainly Moslem youths set buildings and churches ablaze.

Hundreds of troops patrolled the town of Tasikmalaya, some 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Jakarta, after Thursday's violence, apparently sparked by a report of police brutality towards a Moslem teacher.
The town was quiet, with Moslems attending Friday prayers in the mosques and then dispersing peacefully.

Suharto, who heads the world's most populous Moslem nation, said in a post-Christmas speech in Jakarta prepared for delivery to Christians in the civil service and military that there had been civil and political unrest during the past year.
"We thank God that in the end we have succeeded in overcoming that unrest," he said.
A total of 25 churches and a temple were burned by Moslems near Surabaya in East Java last October over a case in which a Moslem heretic was subsequently jailed for blasphemy against Islam.

Jakarta itself suffered its worst riots in more than two decades in July in violence triggered by infighting for control of the minority Indonesian Democratic Party, one of only three groups permitted to contest general elections next May.
A military official and local journalists said at least two people -- one a middle-aged ethnic Chinese woman carried from a burnt out shop -- had died in Thursday's rioting in Tasikmalaya.

A policeman said the riot apparently had been sparked by a report that police had beaten teachers from an Islamic school. Local news reports said one of the teachers had disciplined the son of a policeman, who summoned them for questioning.

Car showrooms, banks and stores owned by ethnic Chinese as well as Christian churches were the main targets. The Indonesian Legal Aid Institute, which sent a team to the town, said 13 churches and seven schools had been burnt.
Suharto said in his speech that the disturbances this year should strengthen the resolve of religious people "to maintain and strengthen the nation's unity and cohesion".
"I believe that most religious people in this country are able to control themselves in facing various religious issues that develop in society," he said.
But he said people should be on their guard against groups in society who could cause trouble among the various religions.
"Religious people should be mature and practise self-restraint, avoiding activities that can create resentment among other people," he said.
While more than 80 percent of Indonesia's nearly 200 million people are Moslems, the state recognises the world's major religions.
In Tasikmalaya, military authorities said 126 people had been detained for questioning. The legal aid institute said 160 people were being held.
Local residents put up signs on their premises and vehicles saying "Owned by Moslem" to save their property.

Rioters had scrawled obscenities on walls against the ethnic Chinese -- seen as dominating the economic life of the town. The rioters had also written signs saying "No to Jesus," "No to the Jews", and "Police are super-corrupt".
Abdurrahman Wahid, leader of the Nahdlatul Ulama, Indonesia's largest Moslem organisation with some 30 million members, condemned the violence and called for calm.
